source.title: Phonological Abstraction and Exception Memorization in Noisy Tone Learning
source.authors: Yi Yang; Yi-Ming Wang; Jia-Hong Yuan

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Tests noisy-label learning dynamics in a speech model on tone classification, with scale, capacity, checkpoint, and perturbation conditions; this is a new modality and task setting for the claim.
record.gate_note: The study replaces tone labels at varying rates, tracks training fit and clean test accuracy, and reports capacity and perturbation outcomes. Results cited from other work, including the original image-classification findings, are not rows. The supplied text reports only selected numeric trajectory and perturbation results; do not infer precise values from figures. No training-time comparison is reported.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures noisy-label fitting, clean generalization across corruption levels, and learning order in speech transformers, bearing on V4 and V6. It never completely randomizes the training labels, so it does not test V1 as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that recoverable tone-learning settings exhibit shared-pattern learning before exception fitting, including without pretraining and under reduced capacity. Extreme noise can prevent reliable recovery. They additionally conclude that acoustic compression does not selectively remove memorization, and that fitted exceptions are locally more fragile than abstraction-consistent predictions.
record.recipe_differences: Uses pretrained wav2vec2.0/HuBERT speech models on Mandarin tone classification with syllable-level random label replacement, instead of standard image classifiers trained on true versus completely random labels. Fine-tuning uses Adam, a staged freeze/unfreeze schedule, and a frozen convolutional feature encoder; the paper also varies training scale and introduces capacity constraints. It does not compare training times for true versus random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Training scale and label-replacement ratio change clean test accuracy; continued training can degrade test accuracy and self-correction in the 70% replacement condition; depth and rank constraints change outcomes; best-validation versus last checkpoints differ; perturbation strength and type change local retention/correction.

fits_no_version.finding: Fitted exceptions are less robust to waveform perturbations than clean-label predictions; perturbations can restore clean predictions in recoverable conditions but often fail under heavy label noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorized noisy labels occupy less perturbation-stable input neighborhoods than shared-pattern predictions, with clean-label recoverability depending on the training regime.

record.peer_reviewed: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
record.problems: Results are single-run percentages with no reported error bars or significance tests. The paper uses Mandarin tone classification as a proxy, does not test completely random labeling of all examples or image classifiers, and does not report training-time ratios. Several trajectory and perturbation values are figure-only. Some conditions report best-checkpoint test accuracy rather than final test accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out for the 60-row cap. Figure-only sweep details beyond the reported qualitative text are not converted into numeric rows.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling and its training-fit/chance-test outcome are untested. Replacement stops at 90% of tone-bearing targets, can resample the original label, and leaves silence targets unchanged. No fully random versus true-label comparison with identical settings is provided.
No time-to-fit or convergence-time ratio between true and random labels, or systematic corruption-dependent convergence comparison, is reported.
No training on shuffled, independently permuted, or Gaussian-noise inputs. Post-training waveform perturbations do not test this version.

The fully randomized endpoint and perfect final training fit throughout the entire scale–noise grid are untested or unreported. Most landscape values are selected-checkpoint test accuracies rather than paired final training and test measurements.
No controlled removal or addition of weight decay, dropout, or training data augmentation tests either part of this version. Rank constraints do not substitute for these comparisons.
No separate completely random-label training condition is compared with real-label training. The evidence concerns learning order within partially corrupted speech datasets.

missing.what: Clean baselines and matched noise sequences for the main landscape. At 100% scale, accuracies for 0%–90% replacement are 94.7, 94.2, 93.6, 93.2, 92.8, 91.0, 87.4, 85.4, 46.5, 20.5%. At 50% scale, 50% to 60% replacement increases accuracy from 87.5% to 88.8%, showing that the trend is not strictly monotonic.
Final training accuracy of 100.0% for the two-layer, 100%-scale, 50%-replacement run; final test accuracies of 58.7% and 56.1% for the six- and four-layer 50%-scale, 50%-replacement runs.

Rank-intervention noise sweeps beyond the extracted 50% column. For rank 2, test accuracy across 50%, 60%, 70%, 80% replacement is 79.9, 76.1, 67.6, 46.6%; for rank 64 it is 87.6, 85.3, 82.5, 36.4%. These expose how capacity changes the degradation profile.

record.verdict_notes: This is not an original source for any version. Image classification is not a required condition of the supplied claim versions. Nominal replacement differs from actual changed-label rate: uniform replacement can retain the original tone, and silence labels are never replaced. Reported near-chance performance is the authors' characterization, not a verified universal 20% baseline, because evaluation includes silence and imbalanced labels. Results are single runs without reported uncertainty. Deliberately corrupting labels is the experimental manipulation relevant to V4 and V6, rather than an exclusion for purpose-induced behavior.

versions.untested_parts: Image classification, completely random labeling of all examples, chance test error, and unchanged original architecture or hyperparameters are not tested; the study uses Mandarin speech, replacement ratios through 90%, and pretrained speech-model fine-tuning.

The paper reports selected scale/noise conditions and test accuracies, not a complete numeric training-error trajectory for every noise ratio. Noise replacement is applied to tone-bearing training labels; 100% replacement is not tested.

The study examines tone-label self-correction and memorization in noisy Mandarin speech, not image classification or the specific real-versus-random-label comparison of Arpit et al. It does not compare with a completely randomized labeling condition.
